relevance_reason: Only the title ("Written in our genes?") was available, with no abstract or full text. The title says nothing about Parkinson disease, genes, variants or patients, so no quotable finding can be taken from it. It looks like a commentary that probably gives only general context.
Clinical cohort study of 276 PD patients identifying a family history of dementia and lower MMSE scores as risk factors for hallucinations in PD. This is a phenotype detail a curator might cite.

findings.statement: Paleacu et al. (2005) studied 276 outpatients with Parkinson disease and found hallucinations in 32% of them. In a stepwise logistic regression, risk factors for hallucinations were Mini-Mental State Examination score (p < 0.0001) and a positive family history of dementia (p = 0.0005). The authors concluded that a family history of dementia and lower MMSE scores are risk factors for hallucinations in PD.
quotes: Hallucinations were present in 32% of the 276 patients. Risk factors for hallucinations included Mini-Mental State Examination score (p < 0.0001) and positive family history of dementia (p = 0.0005).
Family history of dementia and lower Mini-Mental State Examination scores are risk factors for hallucinations in Parkinson disease.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It points to a historical or literary discussion of parkinsonism in Shakespeare, which could support only a historical note.

findings.statement: Stien (2005) discussed descriptions of parkinsonism in the works of Shakespeare.
quotes: Shakespeare on parkinsonism.

relevance_reason: Case-control association study showing that GBA mutations (heterozygous carriers of Gaucher disease) are enriched among Ashkenazi Jewish patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease; evidence for GBA as a susceptibility factor for PD.

findings.statement: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) screened 99 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, 74 Ashkenazi patients with Alzheimer disease, and 1,543 healthy Ashkenazi controls for the 6 GBA mutations most common among Ashkenazi Jews (N370S, L444P, 84GG, IVS+1, V394L, and R496H). Thirty-one PD patients (31.3%) had 1 or 2 mutant GBA alleles: 23 were heterozygous for N370S, 4 heterozygous for 84GG, 3 homozygous for N370S, and 1 heterozygous for R496H, compared with 4.1% of Alzheimer patients and 6.2% of controls being Gaucher carriers.
quotes: Thirty-one patients with Parkinson's disease (31.3 percent; 95 percent confidence interval, 22.2 to 40.4 percent) had one or two mutant GBA alleles: 23 were heterozygous for N370S, 4 were heterozygous for 84GG, 3 were homozygous for N370S, and 1 was heterozygous for R496H.

Ninety-five carriers of Gaucher's disease were identified among the 1543 control subjects (6.2 percent; 95 percent confidence interval, 5.0 to 7.4 percent): 92 were heterozygous for N370S, and 3 were heterozygous for 84GG.

findings.statement: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) found that Ashkenazi Jewish patients with Parkinson disease had significantly greater odds of being Gaucher disease (GBA mutation) carriers than patients with Alzheimer disease (odds ratio 10.8; P less than 0.001) or controls (odds ratio 7.0; P less than 0.001), and suggested that heterozygosity for a GBA mutation may predispose Ashkenazi Jews to PD.
quotes: Patients with Parkinson's disease had significantly greater odds of being carriers of Gaucher's disease than did patients with Alzheimer's disease (odds ratio, 10.8; 95 percent confidence interval, 3.0 to 46.6; P<0.001) or control subjects (odds ratio, 7.0; 95 percent confidence interval, 4.2 to 11.4; P<0.001).
Our results suggest that heterozygosity for a GBA mutation may predispose Ashkenazi Jews to Parkinson's disease.

findings.statement: Aharon-Peretz et al. (2004) found that among Ashkenazi PD patients, GBA mutation carriers had a younger age at onset than noncarriers (mean 60.0 vs 64.2 years; P = 0.04).
quotes: Among the patients with Parkinson's disease, patients who were carriers of Gaucher's disease were younger than those who were not carriers (mean [+/-SD] age at onset, 60.0+/-14.2 years vs. 64.2+/-11.7 years; P=0.04).

phenotypes.text: earlier age at onset of Parkinson disease

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It is a review or commentary on the genetics of Parkinson disease, but without an abstract or full text it reports no specific patients, variants or data that could support a finding.

Population-based twin study that estimated how much of late-onset PD is heritable. The authors found low concordance and that environmental factors mattered most, which is relevant to the inheritance section.

findings.statement: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004) studied PD in same-sex and opposite-sex twin pairs from the Swedish Twin Registry. They screened 33,780 twins in 14,082 pairs by telephone interview and by linkage to the Swedish Inpatient Discharge Register. They identified 247 twins with possible PD and 517 with suspected parkinsonism or movement disorder. For possible PD there were only 2 concordant pairs, both female and dizygotic. Concordance stayed low in all zygosity groups when the definition of affected was broadened.
quotes: The authors screened 33,780 twins in 14,082 pairs for PD by telephone interviews and linked the STR to the Swedish Inpatient Discharge Register.
For possible PD, there were only two concordant pairs, both female dizygotic.
Similarly, concordances were low in all zygosity groups when the definition of affected was expanded to include twins with suspected parkinsonism or movement disorder in addition to possible PD.

findings.statement: Wirdefeldt et al. (2004) found that the best-fitting structural equation model included only environmental components of variance. Results suggested a slightly larger familial component in women. The authors concluded that environmental factors are most important in the etiology of PD and that genetic effects in PD are notably less important than in other complex diseases.
quotes: Sex differences in the relative importance of genetic and environmental effects were indicated with a marginally larger familial component in women. The best-fitting structural equation model included only environmental components of variance.
These results suggest that environmental factors are most important in the etiology of PD. Compared with other complex diseases, the importance of genetic effects in PD is notably low.

relevance_reason: Population-based prevalence study of Parkinson disease in Singapore comparing Chinese, Malay, and Indian ethnic groups; relevant to population genetics section.

findings.statement: Tan et al. (2004) carried out a 3-phase door-to-door community survey of a random sample of 15,000 people aged 50 years and older (9,000 Chinese, 3,000 Malays, 3,000 Indians) in central Singapore, with a 67% participation rate. They identified 46 people with Parkinson disease, 16 of whom had not been diagnosed before. The prevalence of PD in people aged 50 and older was 0.30% (age-adjusted to the 1970 US census) and rose significantly with age. Age-adjusted prevalence was the same in Chinese (0.33%), Malays (0.29%), and Indians (0.28%) (p = 1.0). The authors concluded that prevalence was comparable to that in Western countries and suggested that environmental factors may be more important than racially determined genetic factors in the development of PD.
quotes: Forty-six participants with PD were identified of which 16 were newly diagnosed cases. The prevalence rate of PD for those aged 50 and above in Singapore was 0.30% (95% CI: 0.22 to 0.41), age-adjusted to US 1970 census.
The age-adjusted prevalence rates among Chinese (0.33%, 95% CI: 0.22 to 0.48), Malays (0.29%, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.67), and Indians (0.28%, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.67) were the same (p = 1.0).
Environmental factors may be more important than racially determined genetic factors in the development of PD.

relevance_reason: Reports an association of GSTO1 and GSTO2 at the chromosome 10q age-at-onset linkage region with age at onset of Parkinson disease (and Alzheimer disease), so it is modifier evidence for late-onset PD.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2003) used 'genomic convergence' to prioritize candidate genes in a 15-cM region on chromosome 10q that they had previously linked to age at onset in Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease. Expression studies of hippocampus from AD patients and controls found 4 genes in the linkage region whose expression differed significantly: stearoyl-CoA desaturase, NDUFB8, PRSS11, and GSTO1.
quotes: We previously reported genetic linkage of loci controlling age-at-onset in Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) to a 15 cM region on chromosome 10q.

Analysis revealed that four of the genes [stearoyl-CoA desaturase; NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase 1 beta subcomplex 8; protease, serine 11; and glutathione S-transferase, omega-1 (GSTO1)] were significantly different in their expression between AD and controls and mapped to the 10q age-at-onset linkage region

findings.statement: In allelic association studies of age at onset using 1,362 samples from a PD dataset (635 PD patients) and 2,814 samples from an AD dataset (1,773 AD patients), Li et al. (2003) found no association for 3 of the candidate genes. They did find a significant association for GSTO1 (P = 0.007) and for the neighbouring gene GSTO2 (P = 0.005). They noted that GSTO1 may be involved in the posttranslational modification of interleukin-1-beta, which they called provocative given reports that inflammation may play a role in these disorders.
quotes: Using 2814 samples from our AD dataset (1773 AD patients) and 1362 samples from our PD dataset (635 PD patients), allelic association studies for age-at-onset effects in AD and PD revealed no association for three of the candidates
but a significant association was found for GSTO1 (P=0.007) and a second transcribed member of the GST omega class, GSTO2 (P=0.005), located next to GSTO1.
recent data suggest that GSTO1 maybe involved in the post-translational modification of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1beta.

relevance_reason: Family aggregation study estimating PD risk in first-degree relatives of early- and late-onset PD probands; provides inheritance evidence for late-onset PD.

findings.statement: Marder et al. (2003) estimated PD risk in first-degree relatives of 221 PD probands with onset at age 50 years or younger and 266 probands with onset after age 50, compared with first-degree relatives of 409 control probands. Risk was similarly increased among first-degree relatives of early-onset probands (risk ratio (RR) 2.9; 95% CI 1.6-5.0) and late-onset probands (RR 2.7; 95% CI 1.6-4.4).
quotes: We estimated the degree of increased risk of PD in first-degree relatives of 221 PD probands with age of onset 50 years or younger and 266 PD probands with age of onset older than 50 years compared with the first-degree relatives of 409 control probands.

Risk of PD was similar among first-degree relatives of early-onset PD probands (risk ratio [RR], 2.9; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.6-5.0; p = 0.0002) and late-onset PD probands (RR, 2.7; 95% CI, 1.6-4.4; p = 0.0002)

findings.statement: Marder et al. (2003) found that in late-onset PD families, both siblings (RR 3.6; 95% CI 1.3-10.3) and parents (RR 2.5; 95% CI 1.4-4.6) of probands were at increased risk compared with control relatives, whereas in early-onset families siblings (RR 7.9) but not parents (RR 1.7, not significant) were at increased risk. They concluded this pattern was consistent with an autosomal recessive contribution to early-onset but not late-onset PD, and that genetic factors are important in both, but the specific genes and mode of inheritance may differ.
quotes: In late-onset families, both siblings (RR, 3.6; 95% CI, 1.3-10.3; p = 0.02) and parents (RR, 2.5; 95% CI, 1.4-4.6; p = 0.003) were at increased risk compared with control relatives.
This pattern is consistent with an autosomal recessive contribution to the inheritance of early but not late-onset PD.
Genetic factors are important in both early- and late-onset PD, but specific genes and mode of inheritance may differ between the two groups.

relevance_reason: Early report of familial parkinsonism suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance; only the title is available.

findings.statement: SPELLMAN (1962) reported familial cases of parkinsonism and presented evidence of a dominant trait in a patient's family.
quotes: Report of familial cases of parkinsonism. Evidence of a dominant trait in a patient's family.

relevance_reason: Genome-wide linkage study in 362 multiplex PD families reporting susceptibility loci on chromosomes 2, X, 10 and 14 and evidence for gene-by-gene interactions; adds mapping evidence for late-onset PD susceptibility.

findings.statement: Pankratz et al. (2003) performed genome-wide nonparametric linkage analysis in 754 affected individuals comprising 425 sib pairs from 362 multiplex Parkinson disease families. Under a model restricted to individuals with verified PD (216 sib pairs), the maximum lod score was 3.4 on chromosome 2; under a model including all affected individuals (425 sib pairs), a lod score of 3.1 was obtained on the X chromosome.
quotes: We studied 754 affected individuals, comprising 425 sibling pairs, to identify PD susceptibility genes.
Model I included only those individuals with a more stringent diagnosis of verified PD (216 sibling pairs) and resulted in a maximum LOD score of 3.4 on chromosome 2.
Model II included all affected individuals (425 sibling pairs) and yielded a LOD score of 3.1 on the X chromosome.

findings.statement: In the 85 families of Pankratz et al. (2003) with a very strong family history of PD, a genome screen gave strong evidence of linkage to chromosome 2 (lod = 4.9) and also a lod score of 2.4 on chromosome 14. In the 277 families without a strong family history, linkage was detected to chromosomes 10 (lod = 2.4) and X (lod = 3.2). The authors concluded that there was consistent evidence of linkage to chromosomes 2 and X.
quotes: The 85 families with a very strong family history of PD were employed in a genome screen and, in addition to strong evidence of linkage to chromosome 2 (LOD=4.9), also produced a LOD of 2.4 on chromosome 14.
A genome screen performed in the 277 families without a strong family history of PD detected linkage to chromosomes 10 (LOD=2.4) and X (LOD=3.2).
These findings demonstrate consistent evidence of linkage to chromosomes 2 and X

findings.statement: Pankratz et al. (2003) screened the parkin gene in a subset of families with earlier onset or positive lod scores at a parkin marker. A genome screen in the 23 families with PD patients carrying a mutation in only one parkin allele detected evidence of linkage to chromosome 10 (lod = 2.3). The authors concluded that their findings supported the hypothesis that gene-by-gene (epistatic) interactions are important in PD susceptibility.
quotes: Screening of the parkin gene was performed in a subset of the sample having earlier age of PD onset or a positive LOD score with a marker in the parkin gene.
A genome screen using the 23 families with PD patients having a mutation in only one allele of the parkin gene detected evidence of linkage to chromosome 10 (LOD=2.3).
also support the hypothesis that gene-by-gene interactions are important in PD susceptibility.

relevance_reason: Animal model study: genome-wide expression profiling in alpha-synuclein transgenic Drosophila model of PD.

findings.statement: Scherzer et al. (2003) profiled expression of the entire Drosophila genome at presymptomatic, early, and advanced disease stages in transgenic flies expressing human alpha-synuclein, which replicate age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons, Lewy body-like inclusions, and locomotor impairment. Fifty-one signature transcripts, including lipid, energy, and membrane transport mRNAs, were tightly associated with alpha-synuclein expression, and expression changes revealed specific pathology already at the presymptomatic stage. In age-matched tau transgenic flies, transcription of the alpha-synuclein-associated genes was normal, suggesting highly distinct pathways of neurodegeneration.
quotes: Fifty-one signature transcripts, including lipid, energy and membrane transport mRNAs, were tightly associated with alpha-synuclein expression.
at the pre-symptomatic stage, when the potential for neuroprotection is greatest, expression changes revealed specific pathology
In age-matched tau transgenic Drosophila, the transcription of alpha-synuclein associated genes was normal, suggesting highly distinct pathways of neurodegeneration.

relevance_reason: Case series describing typical Parkinson disease in patients with type 1 Gaucher disease. It adds clinical evidence for the link between Gaucher disease (GBA) and PD.

findings.statement: Bembi et al. (2003) described 4 patients with type 1 Gaucher disease, 2 of whom were sibs, who had typical Parkinson disease. Features included asymmetric onset of rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and a good response to antiparkinsonian therapy. The authors contrasted this with earlier reports, in which PD with Gaucher disease mainly showed bilateral akinetic-rigid signs and a poor response to levodopa.
quotes: The authors describe four patients (two siblings) with type 1 Gaucher disease presenting with the following signs of typical PD: asymmetric onset of rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and a favorable response to Parkinson therapies.
The clinical picture is characterized by the predominance of bilateral akinetic-rigid signs and poor response to levodopa therapy.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication

relevance_reason: Reports a candidate susceptibility variant (R621C) in SNCAIP (synphilin-1) in sporadic PD patients with functional studies; supports the PD entry's molecular genetics/susceptibility section.

findings.statement: Marx et al. (2003) screened the synphilin-1 gene (SNCAIP) in 328 German patients with familial or sporadic PD and identified a heterozygous C-to-T transition at coding position 1861 resulting in an arg621-to-cys (R621C) substitution in 2 apparently sporadic PD patients. The mutation was absent in 702 control chromosomes from healthy Germans.
quotes: we performed a detailed mutation analysis of the synphilin-1 gene in 328 German familial and sporadic PD patients

In two apparently sporadic PD patients we deciphered a novel C to T transition in position 1861 of the coding sequence leading to an amino acid substitution from arginine to cysteine in position 621 (R621C).
This mutation was absent in a total of 702 chromosomes of healthy German controls.

variants.as_reported: R621C (C to T transition in position 1861)

findings.statement: In functional studies in SH-SY5Y cells, Marx et al. (2003) found that synphilin-1 produced cytoplasmic inclusions; under proteasomal inhibition, cells expressing C621 synphilin-1 formed significantly fewer inclusions than cells expressing wildtype synphilin-1, and C621-expressing cells were more susceptible to staurosporine-induced cell death. The authors suggested a causative role for R621C in PD and that inclusion formation may be beneficial, with the mutation sensitizing neurons to cellular stress.
quotes: we observed a significantly reduced number of inclusions in cells expressing C621 synphilin-1 compared with cells expressing wild-type (wt) synphilin-1, when subjected to proteasomal inhibition
C621 synphilin-1 transfected cells were more susceptible to staurosporine-induced cell death than cells expressing wt synphilin-1.
suggest that the formation of intracellular inclusions may be beneficial to cells and that a mutation in synphilin-1 that reduces this ability may sensitize neurons to cellular stress

relevance_reason: Pathogenesis study showing COX-2 upregulation in dopaminergic neurons of PD patients and MPTP mice, with mechanistic and therapeutic implications.

findings.statement: Teismann et al. (2003) found that COX-2, the rate-limiting enzyme in prostaglandin E2 synthesis, was upregulated in brain dopaminergic neurons of both PD patients and MPTP-treated mice. They concluded that COX-2 has a critical role in both the pathogenesis and selectivity of the PD neurodegenerative process.
quotes: COX-2, the rate-limiting enzyme in prostaglandin E(2) synthesis, is up-regulated in brain dopaminergic neurons of both PD and MPTP mice.
This study supports a critical role for COX-2 in both the pathogenesis and selectivity of the PD neurodegenerative process.

findings.statement: In MPTP-treated mice, Teismann et al. (2003) showed that COX-2 induction occurred through a JNK/c-Jun-dependent mechanism. Targeting COX-2 protected against MPTP-induced dopaminergic neurodegeneration not by mitigating inflammation but by preventing formation of the oxidant species dopamine-quinone, which has been implicated in PD pathogenesis.
quotes: COX-2 induction occurs through a JNKc-Jun-dependent mechanism after MPTP administration.
We demonstrate that targeting COX-2 does not protect against MPTP-induced dopaminergic neurodegeneration by mitigating inflammation.
Instead, we provide evidence that COX-2 inhibition prevents the formation of the oxidant species dopamine-quinone, which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of PD.

findings.statement: Teismann et al. (2003) suggested that COX-2 inhibitors may be therapies for PD, because they have a good safety record and can cross the blood-brain barrier.
quotes: Because of the safety record of the COX-2 inhibitors, and their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier, these drugs may be therapies for PD.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It is a review of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, so it gives general context but has no citable patient, variant or experimental data on the page.
Phase 1 clinical trial of direct intraputaminal GDNF infusion in Parkinson disease patients; relevant to the clinical management section.

findings.statement: In a phase 1 safety trial, Gill et al. (2003) delivered glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) directly into the putamen of 5 patients with Parkinson disease. One catheter had to be repositioned, and MRI changes resolved after the GDNF concentration was lowered. After 1 year there were no serious clinical side effects. The off-medication UPDRS motor subscore improved by 39%, and the activities of daily living subscore improved by 61%.
quotes: Here we delivered GDNF directly into the putamen of five Parkinson patients in a phase 1 safety trial.

After one year, there were no serious clinical side effects, a 39% improvement in the off-medication motor sub-score of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) and a 61% improvement in the activities of daily living sub-score.

findings.statement: Gill et al. (2003) reported that during chronic intraputaminal GDNF delivery, medication-induced dyskinesias fell by 64% and did not occur off medication. PET scans of [18F]dopamine uptake showed a significant 28% increase in putamen dopamine storage after 18 months, which the authors suggested reflected a direct effect of GDNF on dopamine function.
quotes: Medication-induced dyskinesias were reduced by 64% and were not observed off medication during chronic GDNF delivery.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scans of [(18)F]dopamine uptake showed a significant 28% increase in putamen dopamine storage after 18 months, suggesting a direct effect of GDNF on dopamine function.

relevance_reason: A review of the genetic and environmental factors behind Parkinson disease. It reports no original patients or variants, but it summarizes how genetic and environmental factors may interact in causing the disease.

findings.statement: In a review, Warner and Schapira (2003) summarized evidence for a genetic role in Parkinson disease from twin and family studies, from mapping and cloning PARK genes, and from studies of possible susceptibility genes. They also reviewed evidence that environmental factors may play a part. They concluded that most cases probably result from a complex interplay between genetic and environmental influences.
quotes: In recent years, however, there has been increasing evidence to support a role for genetic factors in its cause. This has come from twin and family studies, the mapping and cloning of PARK genes that are associated with the development of PD, and analysis of potential susceptibility genes.
It is likely that for most cases, there is a complex interplay between these genetic and environmental influences in the causation of Parkinson's disease.

relevance_reason: Case-control association study of NAT2 slow acetylator genotype as a susceptibility factor for PD in Hong Kong Chinese.

findings.statement: Chan et al. (2003) studied 99 Chinese patients with PD and 126 controls from 2 Hong Kong hospitals and used PCR-RFLP to genotype the M1, M2, and M3 slow acetylator polymorphisms of NAT2. The slow acetylator genotype was much more frequent in patients than in controls (68.7% vs 28.6%), with an odds ratio of 5.53 (95% CI 3.08-9.92) after adjusting for age, sex, and smoking history. In a subgroup analysis, smoking did not change the association. The authors suggested that the association was evidence for a possible functional relationship between the NAT2 slow acetylator genotype and PD.
quotes: PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism was used to identify M1, M2, and M3 mutant polymorphisms of the slow acetylator genotype for N-acetyltransferase 2.

The frequency of the slow acetylator genotype for N-acetyltransferase 2 in the PD group was significantly higher than that of the control group (68.7% vs 28.6%) with an OR of 5.53 (95% CI 3.08 to 9.92) after adjusting for age, sex, and smoking history.
In a subgroup analysis smoking had no modifying effect on the association between genotype and PD.

relevance_reason: An association study finding that mtDNA haplogroups J and K and the 10398G SNP in ND3 lower the risk of Parkinson disease in white individuals. This is susceptibility evidence for the entry.

findings.statement: van der Walt et al. (2003) genotyped 10 SNPs that define the European mtDNA haplogroups in 609 white patients with PD and 340 unaffected white controls. People in haplogroup J (OR 0.55; 95% CI 0.34-0.91; P = 0.02) or haplogroup K (OR 0.52; 95% CI 0.30-0.90; P = 0.02) had a significantly lower risk of PD than people in the most common haplogroup, H.
quotes: we genotyped 10 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that define the European mtDNA haplogroups in 609 white patients with PD and 340 unaffected white control subjects

individuals classified as haplogroup J (odds ratio [OR] 0.55; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.34-0.91; P=.02) or K (OR 0.52; 95% CI 0.30-0.90; P=.02) demonstrated a significant decrease in risk of PD versus individuals carrying the most common haplogroup, H

findings.statement: van der Walt et al. (2003) found that 10398G, an mtDNA SNP that defines haplogroups J and K, was strongly associated with a lower risk of PD (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.39-0.73; P = 0.0001). This SNP changes threonine to alanine, a nonconservative substitution, in the ND3 subunit of complex I. After stratifying by sex, the protective effect appeared stronger in women (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.27-0.71; P = 0.0009). The authors suggested that ND3 is an important factor in PD susceptibility among white individuals.
quotes: a specific SNP that defines these two haplogroups, 10398G, is strongly associated with this protective effect (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.39-0.73; P=.0001)
SNP 10398G causes a nonconservative amino acid change from threonine to alanine within the NADH dehydrogenase 3 (ND3) of complex I
After stratification by sex, this decrease in risk appeared stronger in women than in men (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.27-0.71; P=.0009)

findings.statement: van der Walt et al. (2003) found that SNP 9055A in the mitochondrial ATP6 gene had a protective effect against PD in women (OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.22-0.93; P = 0.03).
quotes: SNP 9055A of ATP6 demonstrated a protective effect for women (OR 0.45; 95% CI 0.22-0.93; P=.03)

relevance_reason: Case series of patients with Gaucher disease and parkinsonism, which supports GBA as a susceptibility/modifier factor for Parkinson disease; this is context for the late-onset PD entry.

findings.statement: Várkonyi et al. (2003) reported 4 adult patients with type 1 Gaucher disease who also had parkinsonism. Their parkinsonian signs began relatively early, progressed quickly, and did not respond to therapy.
quotes: We report the simultaneous occurrence of Gaucher disease with parkinsonian in four adult patients.
The patients had a relatively early onset of parkinsonian manifestations, and their disease was rapidly progressive and refractory to therapy.

findings.statement: Várkonyi et al. (2003) found that each of the 4 patients with both Gaucher disease and parkinsonism had a different Gaucher genotype, and that 4 of the alleles carried the common N370S mutation. No mutations were found in the parkin or alpha-synuclein genes. The authors suggested that the two phenotypes occur together because of a shared pathway, a modifier, or another genetic cause.
quotes: Each had a different Gaucher genotype, although four alleles carried the common N370S mutation.
No mutations were identified in the genes for parkin or alpha-synuclein.
suggests a shared pathway, modifier, or other genetic etiology.

relevance_reason: Case-control association study of NOS1 (nNOS) and NOS2 (iNOS) polymorphisms with Parkinson disease risk, including an interaction with smoking; it bears on susceptibility to late-onset PD.

findings.statement: In a community-based case-control study of 209 Parkinson disease patients and 488 controls of European (mostly French) ancestry, Levecque et al. (2003) found associations with a polymorphism in exon 22 of iNOS (NOS2) (OR for AA carriers = 0.50, 95% CI 0.29-0.86, P = 0.01) and a polymorphism in exon 29 of nNOS (NOS1) (OR for T allele carriers = 1.53, 95% CI 1.08-2.16, P = 0.02). They found no association with a polymorphism in exon 18 of nNOS (OR for T allele carriers = 1.20, P = 0.30). Subjects were enrolled through the Mutualite Sociale Agricole, the French health insurance organization for agricultural workers, and controls were matched for age, sex and region of residence.
quotes: Two-hundred and nine PD patients and 488 controls of European (mostly French) ancestry and matched for age, sex and region of residency were included in this study.

Associations were observed with polymorphisms present in exon 22 of iNOS (OR for AA carriers=0.50, 95% CI=0.29-0.86, P=0.01) and in exon 29 of nNOS (OR for carriers of the T allele=1.53, 95% CI=1.08-2.16, P=0.02)
no association was observed with a polymorphism in exon 18 of nNOS (OR for carriers of the T allele=1.20, 95% CI=0.85-1.69, P=0.30)

variants.as_reported: polymorphism in exon 29 of nNOS (T allele)
polymorphism in exon 18 of nNOS (T allele)

findings.statement: Levecque et al. (2003) found a significant interaction between the nNOS polymorphisms and current or past cigarette smoking (nNOS exon 18, P = 0.05; nNOS exon 29, P = 0.04). They concluded that the data favor NOS1 and NOS2 as new modifier genes in PD.
quotes: a significant interaction of the nNOS polymorphisms with current and ever cigarette smoking was found (nNOS 18, P=0.05; nNOS 29, P=0.04)
All together, these data favour an involvement of these two genes as new modifier genes in PD.

relevance_reason: Association study linking the IL1B -511 polymorphism to Parkinson disease in Finnish patients; only the title was available.

findings.statement: Mattila et al. (2002) reported an association between a polymorphism at position -511 in the interleukin-1-beta gene (IL1B) and Parkinson disease in Finnish patients.
quotes: Association of an interleukin 1B gene polymorphism (-511) with Parkinson's disease in Finnish patients.

relevance_reason: Genome-wide linkage screen in PD sib pairs without parkin mutations; reports suggestive linkage to chromosomes X, 2, 4, 5, 13. It is supporting mapping evidence for late-onset PD susceptibility loci.

findings.statement: Pankratz et al. (2002) studied 203 PD sib pairs who had a rigorous neurologic assessment. They excluded 22 families with parkin mutations and ran a genome screen with multipoint nonparametric linkage analysis in 160 multiplex families. With verified PD only (model I; 96 sib pairs from 90 families), the highest lod scores were on chromosome X (2.1) and chromosome 2 (1.9). With all examined individuals counted as affected (model II; 170 sib pairs from 160 families), the lod scores rose to 2.7 for chromosome X and 2.5 for chromosome 2.
quotes: Thus, a total of 160 multiplex families without evidence of a parkin mutation were used in multipoint nonparametric linkage analysis to identify PD-susceptibility genes.
Under model I, the highest LOD scores were observed on chromosome X (LOD score 2.1) and on chromosome 2 (LOD score 1.9).
Analyses performed with all available sibling pairs (model II) found even greater evidence of linkage to chromosome X (LOD score 2.7) and to chromosome 2 (LOD score 2.5).

findings.statement: Pankratz et al. (2002) also found evidence of linkage to chromosomes 4, 5, and 13, with lod scores above 1.5. They noted that these results agreed with other linkage studies that had reported linkage to chromosomes 5 and X.
quotes: Evidence of linkage was also found to chromosomes 4, 5, and 13 (LOD scores >1.5).
Our findings are consistent with those of other linkage studies that have reported linkage to chromosomes 5 and X.

findings.statement: Pankratz et al. (2002) identified parkin mutations in 22 of the PD sib-pair families after prioritizing families with positive lod scores for a marker in a parkin intron. They excluded these families from the genome screen to reduce genetic heterogeneity.
quotes: Families with positive LOD scores for a marker in an intron of the parkin gene were prioritized for parkin-gene testing, and mutations in the parkin gene were identified in 22 families.
To reduce genetic heterogeneity, these families were not included in subsequent genome-screen analysis.

relevance_reason: Segregation analysis of 948 PD index case families providing evidence for a rare major Mendelian gene influencing PD age of onset and susceptibility.

findings.statement: Maher et al. (2002) performed segregation analysis on the nuclear families of 948 consecutively ascertained PD index cases from 3 US centers (University of Virginia, UMDNJ-Robert Wood Johnson, and Boston University). The analyses supported the presence of a rare major Mendelian gene for PD in both age-of-onset and susceptibility models; the age-of-onset model suggested a gene influencing age-dependent penetrance rather than susceptibility, and it was not evident whether the two analyses modeled the same gene or different genes.
quotes: We collected information involving the nuclear families of 948 consecutively ascertained PD index cases
These analyses support the presence of a rare major Mendelian gene for PD in both the age-of-onset and susceptibility model.
It is not evident whether these two analyses are modeling the same gene or different genes with different effects on PD.

findings.statement: In the 948 PD index cases studied by Maher et al. (2002), 60.4% were male and 39.6% female, with a mean age of onset of 57.7 years; affected relatives included fathers (4.7%), mothers (6.6%), brothers (2.9%), and sisters (3.2%), proportions similar across the 3 sites. While most index cases were male, modestly more reported affected relatives were female.
quotes: The proportion of male (60.4%) and female (39.6%) cases, the mean age of onset (57.7 years), and the proportion of affected fathers (4.7%), mothers (6.6%), brothers (2.9%), and sisters (3.2%) were similar across the three sites.
While most of the index cases were male, modestly more of the reported affected relatives were female.

findings.statement: Maher et al. (2002) suggested that the significant genes influencing PD penetrance may interact with environmental factors or other genes, and that such gene-environment interactions involving reduced penetrance may explain the low concordance rates among monozygotic twins for PD.
quotes: Such gene environment interactions, involving reduced penetrance in PD, may explain the low concordance rates among monozygotic twins for this disease.

relevance_reason: Genome screen for age-at-onset modifier loci in PD families; linkage to 1p and 10q for AAO.

findings.statement: Li et al. (2002) performed a genomic screen for age at onset (AAO) in 174 families with Parkinson disease and 449 families with Alzheimer disease. Heritability of AAO was 40 to 60% in both data sets. For PD, they found significant evidence for linkage of AAO to chromosome 1p (lod = 3.41).
quotes: a genomic screen was performed for AAO in families with Alzheimer disease (AD; n=449) and Parkinson disease (PD; n=174)
Heritabilities between 40%--60% were found in both the AD and PD data sets.
For PD, significant evidence for linkage to AAO was found on chromosome 1p (LOD = 3.41).

findings.statement: Li et al. (2002) identified evidence for AAO linkage on chromosomes 6 and 10 independently in both the AD and PD data sets; unified analysis identified a single peak on chromosome 10q between D10S1239 and D10S1237 (maximum lod score 2.62). The authors suggested that a common gene affects age at onset in these two neurodegenerative diseases.
quotes: evidence for AAO linkage on chromosomes 6 and 10 was identified independently in both the AD and PD data sets
Subsequent unified analyses of these regions identified a single peak on chromosome 10q between D10S1239 and D10S1237, with a maximum LOD score of 2.62.
These data suggest that a common gene affects AAO in these two common complex neurodegenerative diseases.

relevance_reason: Describes a large Old-Order Amish kindred with late-onset, typical idiopathic-like PD, gives the prevalence, shows evidence of inheritance from kinship coefficients, and excludes known PD genes and loci. This suggests a novel gene and genetic heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Racette et al. (2002) described a large, multi-incident Old-Order Amish pedigree with PD. Of 113 examined members, 17 had clinically definite, 6 clinically probable and 23 clinically possible PD. Mean age at onset in the clinically definite subjects was 56.7 years. The phenotype was typical of idiopathic PD: rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability and response to levodopa. Dementia occurred in 6 of the clinically definite subjects, and many had levodopa-related motor complications, including wearing off and dyskinesias.
quotes: The authors have examined 113 members of this pedigree and classified 67 as normal (no evidence of PD), 17 as clinically definite PD, 6 as clinically probable PD, and 23 as clinically possible PD. The mean age at onset of the clinically definite subjects was 56.7 years.
The phenotype in this family is typical of idiopathic PD, including rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability, and response to levodopa.
In addition, dementia occurred in six of the clinically definite subjects, and many subjects experienced levodopa-related motor complications including wearing off and dopa-induced dyskinesias.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication

findings.statement: Racette et al. (2002) found that the mean kinship coefficient in Amish subjects with PD or with PD by history (0.036) was significantly higher (p = 0.007) than in age-matched normal Amish controls (0.016). The authors took this as evidence that PD is inherited in this family.
quotes: The mean kinship coefficient in the subjects with PD and those with PD by history (0.036) was higher (p = 0.007) than in a group of age-matched normal Amish control subjects (0.016), providing evidence that PD is inherited in this family.

findings.statement: Racette et al. (2002) calculated a minimum PD prevalence of 552 per 100,000 among people aged 40 years and older in the index Old-Order Amish community. They concluded that PD is more common in this community than in the general population.
quotes: In the index Amish community, a minimum prevalence of PD in the population 40 years and older of 552/100,000 was calculated.
PD in this community is more common than in the general population, and this increased prevalence may be due in part to a novel gene(s).

findings.statement: In the Amish kindred, Racette et al. (2002) sequenced genes with known PD-causing mutations and found no mutations. No single haplotype cosegregated with the disease in any chromosomal region previously linked to PD, and no marker in these regions showed increased homozygosity among definite cases. The authors suggested that the increased prevalence may be due in part to a novel gene or genes.
quotes: Sequence analysis did not detect any mutations in known PD genes. No single haplotype cosegregates with the disease in any of the chromosomal regions previously found to be linked to PD, and no marker in these regions exhibits increased homozygosity among definite PD cases.
this increased prevalence may be due in part to a novel gene(s).

relevance_reason: Drosophila alpha-synuclein model of PD showing Hsp70 chaperone suppression of dopaminergic neuron loss, plus chaperone immunostaining of human Lewy bodies; animal model/pathogenesis evidence.

findings.statement: Auluck et al. (2002) found that directed expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp70 prevented the dopaminergic neuronal loss associated with alpha-synuclein expression in Drosophila, and that interfering with endogenous chaperone activity accelerated alpha-synuclein toxicity.
quotes: We report that directed expression of the molecular chaperone Hsp70 prevented dopaminergic neuronal loss associated with alpha-synuclein in Drosophila and that interference with endogenous chaperone activity accelerated alpha-synuclein toxicity.

findings.statement: Auluck et al. (2002) found that Lewy bodies in human postmortem brain tissue immunostained for molecular chaperones. They suggested that chaperones may play a role in the progression of Parkinson disease.
quotes: Furthermore, Lewy bodies in human postmortem tissue immunostained for molecular chaperones, also suggesting that chaperones may play a role in Parkinson's disease progression.

relevance_reason: Family-based association study implicating MAPT (tau) SNPs and haplotypes as susceptibility factors for idiopathic late-onset PD, following linkage to 17q21.

findings.statement: Martin et al. (2001) tested 5 SNPs within the tau gene (MAPT) for association with idiopathic Parkinson disease using family-based association tests in 1,056 individuals (426 affected, 579 unaffected, 51 with unclear status) from 235 families recruited at 13 clinical centers in the United States and Australia and a family ascertainment core center. Three of the 5 SNPs showed significant association (SNP 3, P = 0.03; SNP 9i, P = 0.04; SNP 11, P = 0.04), whereas SNP 9ii and SNP 9iii did not. Haplotype analysis showed strong evidence of association, with one haplotype positively associated (P = 0.009) and another negatively associated (P = 0.007), and substantial linkage disequilibrium (P less than 0.001) was found among SNPs 3, 9i, 9ii, and 11. The authors concluded that tau is a susceptibility gene for idiopathic PD.
quotes: Among a sample of 1056 individuals from 235 families selected from 13 clinical centers in the United States and Australia and from a family ascertainment core center, we tested 5 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the tau gene for association with PD, using family-based tests of association.
Analysis of association between the SNPs and PD yielded significant evidence of association for 3 of the 5 SNPs tested: SNP 3, P =.03; SNP 9i, P =.04; and SNP 11, P =.04.
Strong evidence of association was found with haplotype analysis, with a positive association with one haplotype (P =.009) and a negative association with another haplotype (P =.007).

findings.statement: Martin et al. (2001) noted that they had previously observed linkage of idiopathic PD to a region on chromosome 17q21 that contains the tau gene, and concluded that this integrated linkage and positional association approach implicated tau as a susceptibility gene for idiopathic PD.
quotes: We recently observed linkage in idiopathic Parkinson disease (PD) to a region on chromosome 17q21 that contains the tau gene.
This integrated approach of genetic linkage and positional association analyses implicates tau as a susceptibility gene for idiopathic PD.

relevance_reason: Genomewide linkage screen in 174 multiplex PD families identifying loci for late-onset PD on 17q, 8p, 5q and 9q.

findings.statement: Scott et al. (2001) performed a complete genomic screen with 344 markers in 174 families with multiple individuals diagnosed with idiopathic PD, ascertained through probands in 13 clinic populations in the continental United States and Australia; 870 family members were studied (378 affected, 379 unaffected, 113 unclear status). Two-point parametric and multipoint nonparametric linkage analysis detected evidence for linkage to chromosomes 17q (MLOD = 2.28; LOD = 2.62), 8p (MLOD = 2.01; LOD = 2.22), and 5q (MLOD = 2.39; LOD = 1.50) overall and in families with late-onset PD, and to chromosome 9q (MLOD = 1.52; LOD = 2.59) in families with both levodopa-responsive and levodopa-nonresponsive patients.
quotes: a complete genomic screen (n = 344 markers) was performed in 174 families with multiple individuals diagnosed as having idiopathic PD, identified through probands in 13 clinic populations in the continental United States and Australia

chromosomes 17q (MLOD = 2.28; LOD = 2.62), 8p (MLOD = 2.01; LOD = 2.22), and 5q (MLOD = 2.39; LOD = 1.50) overall and in families with late-onset PD, and chromosome 9q (MLOD = 1.52; LOD = 2.59) in families with both levodopa-responsive and levodopa-nonresponsive patients

findings.statement: In the genomic screen by Scott et al. (2001), significant linkage to the parkin gene region on chromosome 6 (MLOD = 5.07; LOD = 5.47) was found in families with at least 1 individual with PD onset before age 40 years. The authors concluded that parkin is important in early-onset PD and that multiple genetic factors may be important in idiopathic late-onset PD.
quotes: chromosome 6 in the parkin gene (MLOD = 5.07; LOD = 5.47) in families with at least 1 individual with PD onset at younger than 40 years
Our data suggest that the parkin gene is important in early-onset PD and that multiple genetic factors may be important in the development of idiopathic late-onset PD.

relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with Gaucher disease and parkinsonism carrying GBA mutations, supporting the GBA–parkinsonism association that is relevant to the Parkinson disease entry.

findings.statement: Tayebi et al. (2001) described a woman with mild Gaucher disease and impaired horizontal saccadic eye movements. She developed a tremor at age 42 years, and her gait then deteriorated rapidly. A pallidotomy at age 47 was unsuccessful, and her motor and cognitive decline continued despite enzyme replacement therapy.
quotes: We describe a patient with mild Gaucher disease but impaired horizontal saccadic eye movements who developed a tremor at age 42, followed by rapid deterioration of her gait.
A pallidotomy at age 47 was unsuccessful. Her motor and cognitive deterioration progressed despite enzyme replacement therapy.

findings.statement: In a patient with mild Gaucher disease and parkinsonism, Tayebi et al. (2001) sequenced the glucocerebrosidase gene and found 2 mutations, L444P and D409H. Southern blot analysis showed an extra 17-kb SspI band on the maternal allele. PCR amplification and sequencing showed a duplication that included the glucocerebrosidase pseudogene, the metaxin gene, and a pseudometaxin/metaxin fusion. The authors suggested that gene changes linked to this rearrangement, which arose from a crossover between metaxin and its pseudogene, could contribute to the patient's atypical phenotype.
quotes: Sequencing of the glucocerebrosidase gene identified mutations L444P and D409H.
Southern blot analysis using the enzyme SspI showed that the maternal allele had an additional 17-kb band.
PCR amplifications and sequencing of this fragment demonstrated a duplication which included the glucocerebrosidase pseudogene, metaxin gene, and a pseudometaxin/metaxin fusion.

relevance_reason: A review abstract on the genetics of Parkinson disease. It gives general context (pathology, implicated genes, multifactorial etiology) but no primary data.

findings.statement: Vaughan et al. (2001) reviewed the genetics of parkinsonism, describing idiopathic Parkinson disease as a common progressive neurodegenerative disorder whose pathologic hallmarks are Lewy bodies and massive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. They suggested that nigral degeneration with Lewy body formation may represent a final common pathway of a multifactorial disease process in which both environmental and genetic factors have a role.
quotes: The pathological hallmarks are the presence of Lewy bodies and massive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra.

Nigral degeneration with Lewy body formation and the resulting clinical picture of PD may represent a final common pathway of a multifactorial disease process in which both environmental and genetic factors have a role.

phenotypes.text: loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
phenotypes.hpo_label: Neuronal loss in central nervous system

findings.statement: Vaughan et al. (2001) noted that 2 genes (SNCA and parkin) and 2 further gene loci had been implicated in familial PD, despite large families being rare, heritability in the general population being low, and the disorder being genetically heterogeneous. They also noted that mutations in UCHL1 had been described in familial PD, but that the evidence for its role was less clear.
quotes: Two genes (SNCA and parkin) as well as two gene loci have now been implicated in the pathogenesis of familial PD.
considering the rarity of large families, low heritability in the general population and genetic heterogeneity
Mutations in a further gene, UCHL1, have been described in familial PD although the evidence for its role in PD is less clear.

relevance_reason: A case-control association study of MAOB and COMT polymorphisms and susceptibility to sporadic Parkinson disease in Taiwanese patients, including a gene-gene interaction.

findings.statement: In a case-control study of 224 Taiwanese patients with Parkinson disease and 197 controls matched for age, sex, and birthplace, Wu et al. (2001) found that the MAOB intron 13 G genotype (G in men and G/G in women) was associated with a 2.07-fold increased relative risk of PD. Genotyping was done by PCR-RFLP analysis.
quotes: Two hundred twenty-four patients with PD and 197 controls, matched for age, sex, and birthplace, were recruited.
The MAOB G genotype (G in men and G:/G in women) was associated with a 2.07-fold increased relative risk of PD.

findings.statement: Clarke et al. quotes: The prevalence of Parkinson's disease in individuals older than 65 years was 0.71% (95% confidence interval, 0.19% to 1.23%), with a male predominance (five men, two women).
We investigated the prevalence of PS in a rural Bavarian population of individuals older than 65 years (982 participants; response rate, 82.5%) using a door-to-door-survey and a biphasic approach.

findings.statement: Trenkwalder et al. (1995) found that parkinsonism of other causes in the same elderly German population included drug-induced parkinsonism (4 of 982), vascular parkinsonism (2 of 982), multiple system atrophy (3 of 982), Fahr disease (1 of 982), and an unexpectedly high prevalence of normal-pressure hydrocephalus (4 of 982); 50% of parkinsonism cases were newly diagnosed.
quotes: Parkinsonism of other pathogenesis included drug-induced PS (0.41%, four of 982 inhabitants), vascular PS (0.20%, two of 982), multiple system atrophy (0.31%, three of 982), and Fahr's disease (0.10%, one of 982).

The high prevalence of normal-pressure hydrocephalus (0.41%, four of 982 inhabitants) was an unexpected finding that was confirmed by computed tomography. Fifty percent of cases of PS were newly diagnosed.

relevance_reason: Negative mutation screen of candidate oxidative stress genes (SOD1, SOD2, CAT) in familial and sporadic PD patients; excludes these as PD genes.

findings.statement: Parboosingh et al. (1995) screened 107 unrelated patients with Parkinson disease, from familial and sporadic populations, for mutations in the genes for copper/zinc superoxide dismutase (SOD1), manganese superoxide dismutase (SOD2), and catalase (CAT) using single-strand conformation analysis. They found no mutations and concluded that PD is not caused by mutations in these three free radical detoxifying enzyme genes.
quotes: A total of 107 unrelated patients with PD from two PD populations (familial and sporadic) were screened for mutations in the genes of copper/zinc superoxide dismutase, manganese superoxide dismutase, and catalase by single-strand conformation analysis.
Parkinson's disease is not caused by mutations in the genes of these three detoxifying enzymes.

findings.statement: Parboosingh et al. (1995) identified a glycine-to-aspartic acid substitution in exon 9 of the catalase gene in 1 patient with familial PD, who had decreased red blood cell catalase activity. The authors concluded that this variant was most likely a silent mutation and not the genetic cause of PD in this family.
quotes: we did identify an amino acid substitution (glycine to aspartic acid) in exon 9 of the catalase gene in one patient; decreased red blood cell catalase activity was observed in this patient.
The exon 9 variant in the catalase gene in the one family with PD is most likely a silent mutation and not the genetic cause of PD in this family.

variants.as_reported: glycine to aspartic acid substitution in exon 9

relevance_reason: Twin study evaluating the genetic contribution to Parkinson disease; found zero concordance in monozygotic twins.

findings.statement: Duvoisin et al. (1981) found zero concordance for Parkinson disease in the first 12 monozygotic twin pairs examined in an ongoing twin study. They suggested that genetic factors do not play a major role in the etiology of Parkinson disease.
quotes: Zero concordance for Parkinson disease was found in the first 12 monozygotic twin pairs examined in an ongoing twin study.
These preliminary findings suggest that genetic factors do not play a major role in the etiology of Parkinson disease

findings.statement: In their study of 12 monozygotic twin pairs discordant for Parkinson disease, Duvoisin et al. (1981) noted that one unaffected co-twin had essential tremor, another had cerebrovascular disease, and a third was an alcoholic. Probands appeared to smoke less than co-twins (11.9 vs 16.1 pack-years). Premorbid personality differences between probands and co-twins dated back to late adolescence or early adulthood, which the authors suggested pointed to a prodromal onset of the disease as early as late adolescence or early adult life.
quotes: One co-twin (subject without Parkinson disease) had essential tremor, another had cerebral vascular disease, and a third was an alcoholic.
Cigarette smoking appeared to be less frequent in the probands than in the co-twins (11.9 versus 16.1 pack-years).
There was also evidence of premorbid personality differences between probands and co-twins dating back to late adolescence or early adult years.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It describes a case report of familial Parkinson disease occurring together with familial manic-depressive illness, which is relevant to familial PD and its associated psychiatric features.

findings.statement: Tune et al. (1982) published a case report of familial manic-depressive illness occurring together with familial Parkinson disease.
quotes: Familial manic-depressive illness and familial Parkinson's disease: a case report.

relevance_reason: Clinical/familial study of Parkinson disease patients with onset before age 40. It reports familial aggregation and subgroups, which gives supporting evidence on the genetics of PD.

findings.statement: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) studied 32 patients whose Parkinson disease began before age 40 and identified 3 subgroups: postencephalitic, onset and course with predominant tremor, and onset and course with akinesia and rigidity.
quotes: A pilot study of 32 of our own such cases revealed the existence of 3 subgroups: 1. Post-Encephalitic, 2. Onset and course with predominant tremor, 3. Onset and course with akinesia and rigidity.

findings.statement: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) found familial cases in 46% of patients with Parkinson disease starting before age 40, compared with 10-15% in general Parkinson populations. Patients with tremor onset often had relatives with essential tremor. Patients with akineto-rigid onset often had other relatives with Parkinson disease.
quotes: In this early onset group of patients, there was a 46% incidence of familial cases (as opposed to 10-15% in the general Parkinson populations).
The cases with tremor onset had a high prevalence of essential tremor in their families, while those with an akineto-rigid onset had a high familial incidence of other cases of Parkinson's Disease.

phenotypes.text: family history of essential tremor in tremor-onset cases

findings.statement: Barbeau and Pourcher (1982) reported that familial grey hair, hypertension, diabetes, and thyroid disease appeared more often than expected in the families of patients with early-onset Parkinson disease.
quotes: Familial grey hair, hypertension, diabetes and thyroidopathies appeared to be in higher than expected frequency.

relevance_reason: The paper describes parkinsonism caused by the toxin MPTP. It gives context on the pathogenesis of Parkinson disease, specifically selective damage to the substantia nigra. It does not report any genetic findings.

findings.statement: Langston et al. (1983) described 4 persons who developed marked parkinsonism after intravenous use of an illicit drug. Analysis of the substance injected by 2 of the patients showed mainly 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), with trace amounts of the meperidine analog MPPP. Based on the patients' parkinsonian features and pathologic data from a previously reported case, the authors proposed that MPTP selectively damages cells in the substantia nigra.
quotes: Four persons developed marked parkinsonism after using an illicit drug intravenously.

Analysis of the substance injected by two of these patients revealed primarily 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) with trace amounts of 1-methyl-4-phenyl-4-propionoxy-piperidine (MPPP).
it is proposed that this chemical selectively damages cells in the substantia nigra.

relevance_reason: Twin study assessing concordance of Parkinson disease, used to argue that the main causes of PD are nongenetic; relevant to the inheritance section.

findings.statement: Ward et al. (1983) studied 43 monozygotic (MZ) and 19 dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs in which the index case had definite Parkinson disease. Only one MZ pair was definitely concordant. When pairs with questionable clinical features were included, 4 of 48 MZ pairs and 1 of 19 DZ pairs were concordant. The frequency of PD in MZ cotwins was similar to that expected in an unrelated control group matched for age and sex. The authors concluded that the major factors in the etiology of PD are nongenetic, although they could not identify a single environmental agent.
quotes: Among 43 monozygotic (MZ) and 19 dizygotic (DZ) pairs in which an index case had definite Parkinson's disease (PD), only one MZ pair was definitely concordant for PD.
When pairs with questionable clinical features were included, 4 of 48 MZ and 1 of 19 DZ pairs were concordant.
Although we were unable to identify a single environmental agent, we conclude that the major factors in the etiology of PD are nongenetic.

relevance_reason: Hypothesis paper proposing environmental (possibly toxic) etiology superimposed on age-related neuronal loss in Parkinson disease; context for etiology/pathogenesis discussion.

findings.statement: Calne and Langston (1983) suggested that in most cases of Parkinson disease the cause may be an environmental factor, possibly toxic, superimposed on a background of slow, sustained neuronal loss due to advancing age.
quotes: It is suggested here that in most cases of Parkinson's disease the cause may be an environmental factor, possibly toxic, superimposed on a background of slow, sustained neuronal loss due to advancing age.

relevance_reason: Genetic analysis of Parkinson disease concluding multifactorial etiology; only the title is available.

findings.statement: Kondo et al. (1973) performed a genetic analysis of Parkinson disease and reported evidence of a multifactorial etiology.
quotes: Parkinson's disease. Genetic analysis and evidence of a multifactorial etiology.

relevance_reason: Review of the evidence for and against a hereditary cause of Parkinson disease (family studies, case-control studies, twin concordance). It concludes that heredity has no major role, which is relevant to the inheritance section.

findings.statement: Duvoisin (1987) reviewed the genetics of Parkinson disease. He noted that closer study of the clinical data showed that reported familial clusters of parkinsonism reflected various other disorders, notably olivopontocerebellar atrophy (OPCA) and other forms of multiple system atrophy. He also noted that case-control studies had not found a prevalence of PD among first-degree relatives of index cases significantly higher than in control groups.
quotes: closer study of the clinical data indicates that familial aggregations of parkinsonism have reflected various other disorders, notably OPCA and other forms of multiple system atrophy
Case control studies have failed to document a prevalence of PD among first-degree relatives of index cases significantly exceeding that found in control groups.

findings.statement: Duvoisin (1987) noted that the concordance rate for PD in monozygotic twins had been found to be unexpectedly low and not significantly different from the rate in dizygotic twins or from the prevalence among first-degree relatives. He concluded that the best available data did not support a role of heredity in the etiology of PD, although a nonhereditary, possibly congenital genetic defect was not excluded.
quotes: the concordance rate for PD among monozygotic twins has been found to be unexpectedly low and not significantly different from that among dizygotic twins or the prevalence among first-degree relatives
Thus, the best available data do not support a role of heredity in the etiology of PD. A nonhereditary, possibly congenital genetic defect is, however, not excluded.

findings.statement: Duvoisin (1987) noted that the idea that heredity plays a role in PD came first from positive family histories and reports of kindreds with parkinsonism. He added that it was strengthened by the first systematic family study of PD, carried out by Mjones about 50 years earlier.
quotes: It was initially suggested by positive family histories and later by reports of kindreds of "parkinsonism." It was reinforced by the first systematic family study of PD conducted a half-century ago by Mjones.

relevance_reason: An epidemiologic survey of age-specific prevalence and age at onset of Parkinson disease that suggests onset may be getting earlier, with possible implications for etiology.

findings.statement: Teräväinen et al. (1986) carried out a hospital-based survey of the age-specific prevalence of Parkinson disease in 551 patients from Helsinki and Vancouver. They concluded that the disorder may be starting earlier than it did previously, and they discussed what this might mean for the etiology of Parkinson disease.
quotes: We have conducted a hospital-based survey of the age-specific prevalence of Parkinson's disease in 551 patients from Helsinki and Vancouver.
We conclude that the disorder may be starting earlier than previously and we discuss the implications of this finding for the etiology of Parkinson's disease.

relevance_reason: Reports six families with Parkinson disease and argues from the timing of onset that the familial clustering reflects an environmental rather than genetic cause; relevant to the inheritance/pathogenesis discussion in the PD entry.

findings.statement: Calne et al. (1987) reported 6 families with Parkinson disease in which symptoms tended to begin at about the same calendar time regardless of patient age. Across generations, the mean difference in time of onset was 4.6 years. The mean difference in age at onset between children and parents was 25.2 years. The authors interpreted this pattern as suggesting an environmental rather than a genetic cause.
quotes: We report here six families with Parkinson's disease in whom the onset of symptoms tended to occur at approximately the same time irrespective of the age of the patient.
The mean difference in the time of onset in different generations was 4.6 years while the mean difference in age of onset in children and parents was 25.2 years.
We construe this pattern of age separation within families as suggestive of an environmental rather than genetic cause.

findings.statement: Calne et al. (1987) found no correlation between who developed the disease and degree of consanguinity in their families. They concluded that their findings fit the hypothesis that some cases of Parkinson disease result from early, subclinical environmental damage followed by age-related loss of neurons in the central nervous system.
quotes: Support for this view derives from the lack of correlation between occurrence of the disease and the degree of consanguinity.

We conclude that our findings are in accord with the hypothesis which attributes the cause of some cases of Parkinson's disease to early, subclinical environmental damage followed by age-related attrition of neurons within the central nervous system.

relevance_reason: Case-control study that links defective debrisoquine 4-hydroxylation, a cytochrome P450 function, to susceptibility to Parkinson disease and to earlier onset.

findings.statement: Barbeau et al. (1985) studied debrisoquine 4-hydroxylation, a hepatic cytochrome P450 detoxification function, in 40 patients with Parkinson disease and 40 normal controls. Significantly more parkinsonian patients than controls had partially or totally defective 4-hydroxylation of debrisoquine. Poor metabolizers tended to have had earlier onset of disease. The authors postulated that Parkinson disease results from environmental factors acting on genetically susceptible individuals against a background of normal aging.
quotes: The function of one such system was studied in forty patients with Parkinson's disease and forty normal control subjects.
Significantly more parkinsonian than control subjects had partially or totally defective 4-hydroxylation of debrisoquine.
Poor metabolisers of debrisoquine tended to have had earlier onset of disease.

relevance_reason: Review proposing that mitochondrial DNA defects affecting complex I might play a role in PD pathogenesis; no original patient or variant data.

findings.statement: Di Monte (1991) reviewed evidence that impaired mitochondrial function may underlie neuronal death in Parkinson disease. The evidence included the toxicity of the MPTP metabolite MPP+, which probably acts by blocking mitochondrial electron flow at complex I. It also included reports of reduced mitochondrial complex I activity in the brain and other tissues of parkinsonian patients. Because 7 complex I subunit genes are encoded in the mitochondrial genome, the author suggested that abnormal mtDNA might play a role in PD pathogenesis.
quotes: the toxicity of MPP+ is likely to result from its ability to block mitochondrial electron flow at the level of complex I
recent studies have revealed a deficiency of mitochondrial complex I activity in the brain as well as other tissues of parkinsonian patients
Since seven of these genes are localized in the mitochondrial genome, it is conceivable that abnormal mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) might play a role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease.

relevance_reason: Clinicopathologic study of 100 patients clinically diagnosed with idiopathic PD; addresses diagnostic accuracy and pathology (Lewy bodies), relevant to diagnosis and clinical features sections.

findings.statement: Hughes et al. (1992) reported the pathologic findings in 100 patients diagnosed prospectively by consultant neurologists as having idiopathic Parkinson disease. Seventy-six had nigral Lewy bodies; the 24 without Lewy bodies had diagnoses including progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, Alzheimer disease, Alzheimer-type pathology, and basal ganglia vascular disease. Retrospective application of recommended diagnostic criteria improved diagnostic accuracy to 82%.
quotes: The pathological findings in 100 patients diagnosed prospectively by a group of consultant neurologists as having idiopathic Parkinson's disease are reported. Seventy six had nigral Lewy bodies
In 24 cases without Lewy bodies, diagnoses included progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, Alzheimer's disease, Alzheimer-type pathology, and basal ganglia vascular disease.
The retrospective application of recommended diagnostic criteria improved the diagnostic accuracy to 82%.

findings.statement: Hughes et al. (1992) found that in all 76 patients with clinically diagnosed Parkinson disease who had nigral Lewy bodies, Lewy bodies were also present in the cerebral cortex. The authors suggested that these observations called into question the concept of Parkinson disease as a single distinct morbid entity.
quotes: Seventy six had nigral Lewy bodies, and in all of these Lewy bodies were also found in the cerebral cortex.
These observations call into question current concepts of Parkinson's disease as a single distinct morbid entity.

relevance_reason: Case report of monozygotic twin sisters with concordant Parkinson disease and anosmia, supporting a genetic contribution to PD.

findings.statement: Kissel and Andre (1976) reported monozygotic twin sisters who both developed Parkinson disease and anosmia at age 39 years. The disease was controlled and regressed with L-dopa treatment. The authors noted that 2 families with the same association had been reported previously.
quotes: Monozygotic twin sisters developed Parkinson's disease and anosmia at the age of 39.
The disease was kept under control and regressed with L. Dopa.
Two families with the same association had been previously reported.

findings.statement: Kissel and Andre (1976) suggested that a genetically determined anomaly of dopamine metabolism was probably responsible for the combination of Parkinson disease and anosmia in their monozygotic twins.
quotes: An anomaly of the metabolism of dopamine, genetically determined, is probably responsible for these disorders.

relevance_reason: A family study of how Parkinson disease is inherited. It tests whether the disease follows a multifactorial or an autosomal dominant pattern.

findings.statement: Young et al. (1977) looked at where affected ancestral second-degree relatives fell in the pedigrees of 12 families with Parkinson disease. Affected relatives were on both sides of the family (bilateral) more often than autosomal dominant inheritance would predict. The authors concluded that this pattern suggested a multifactorial cause for most cases of Parkinson disease, but they did not entirely rule out dominant gene inheritance in some families.
quotes: The distribution of ancestral second-degree relatives with Parkinson's disease was evaluated in 12 families. Affected relatives were bilaterally distributed more often than would be expected for autosomal dominance.

The distribution of ancestral secondary cases suggests a multifactorial etiology for most cases of Parkinson's disease. The possibility of dominant gene inheritance in some families is not entirely ruled out.

findings.statement: Kessler (1978) reviewed Parkinson disease from an epidemiologic perspective.
quotes: Parkinson's disease in epidemiologic perspective.
